title: AI Gave Doctors a 'Second Pair of Eyes.' Did Patients Benefit?
hook: A 10,000-visit trial in Kenyan clinics gave clinicians an AI 'second opinion.' It cut their documented errors — but didn't clearly improve how patients actually fared.
key_points: AI Consult, built on OpenAI's GPT-4o, ran in the background as clinicians typed, flagging issues with a green/yellow/red 'traffic light.'
A randomized trial covered nearly 10,000 patient visits across 16 Penda Health clinics in Kenya; results ran in Nature Medicine.
Clinicians using the AI made fewer diagnosis and treatment errors, as graded by expert reviewers.
But the trial found no statistically significant improvement in actual patient outcomes, like unresolved symptoms.
The lesson: better documentation and decisions don't automatically mean patients end up healthier.
It was cheap — about 4 cents per patient — and one clinician credited it with catching a heart defect she might have missed.
content_html: One of the biggest real-world tests of medical AI just reported back, and the result is a useful reality check. Across 16 primary-care clinics in Kenya, clinicians got an AI tool called AI Consult — built on OpenAI's GPT-4o — that watched their notes as they worked and flagged possible mistakes with a simple green-yellow-red "traffic light." It clearly sharpened their paperwork and decisions. Whether patients actually ended up healthier is a murkier story.
extra_html:
The study, published in Nature Medicine and covered by NPR, ran across nearly 10,000 patient visits. Clinicians whose work was double-checked by the AI made fewer errors in diagnosis and treatment, as graded by expert reviewers, and the tool cost only about 4 cents per patient. One clinical officer described catching a possible congenital heart defect in an infant that she says she "would have missed on any other day."

The catch is in the outcomes that matter most. The trial did not find a statistically significant drop in things like unresolved symptoms — the number of bad outcomes was small to begin with, leaving too little signal to be sure the AI moved the needle. It's a distinction worth holding onto as AI spreads through medicine: a tool can measurably improve how care is documented and decided without yet proving that patients are better off. Those are exactly the questions large real-world trials — not accuracy benchmarks — are built to answer.

related.title: An AI-Designed 'Universal' Coronavirus Vaccine
related.hook: A vaccine designed with AI to target a whole virus family — not one strain — passed its first human trial safely and triggered immunity against SARS-CoV-2, SARS, and pandemic-risk bat viruses.
